t: Judge of Israel, or gates of Israel?
p: The Greek says 'they strike the gates of Israel on the cheek'. The Hebrew says the judge of Israel.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the words are visible)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Hebrew makes sense (a ruler shamed) and Mur88 agrees with it. The Greek reading looks like a mistaken or free rendering of the Hebrew word for judge (a translator may have read a similar word for 'gate'). It is also a harder fit with 'cheek'.
b: The Greek of the whole verse is far from the Hebrew ('the daughter will be walled in with a wall'), so the translator may have worked from a damaged or unclear text.

t: Clans, thousands or chiefs?
p: The same letters can be 'thousands' (clans) or, with a waw, 'chiefs'. Matthew 2:6 reads 'leaders'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Qumran scroll 4Q81 (4QXII-f; the transcription prints the word with these consonants); Targum Jonathan (Aramaic)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Vulgate
readings.orig: ἐν χιλιάσιν Ἰούδα; in milibus Iuda

readings.w: Matthew 2:6 (a New Testament quotation, not a manuscript of Micah)

why: The Hebrew word with its plain consonants is printed the same way in the 4Q81 transcription and read the same way by the Greek and Latin as 'thousands'. 'Clans' is the sense of 'thousands' in the passages where Judah is divided into units (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19). Matthew's 'leaders' is a quotation that gives the sense of the line for his purpose, or it reflects reading the same letters as alluf 'chief' (Genesis 36:15); it is not evidence of a different Hebrew text.
b: The Murabba'at scroll is damaged at this word. 'Chief' would need a waw added to the consonants (אלופי), and no Hebrew manuscript has it.

t: Does 4Q81 have an extra 'not'?
p: The transcription of 4Q81 prints an extra word, 'not', between 'for me' and 'come out'. No translation follows it, and its cause is unexplained.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (these words are visible)

Qumran scroll 4Q81 (4QXII-f), as printed in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (ETCBC dataset). The word 'not' is printed without restoration brackets; 'for me' and 'come out' beside it are bracketed (restored)
readings.en: for me not will go out

why: The extra 'not' would reverse the sense and has no other support (not the Greek, the Latin, the Targum or Mur88). Its cause is unexplained: a scribal slip is one suggestion, but a misreading of the damaged surface, a repeated word or an error in the transcription are also possible. No translation follows it.
b: I report only what the transcription prints: one unbracketed word between two bracketed ones. The same scroll appears in the entry above as printing the consonants of alpe as in the Masoretic Text; a scroll can agree with the Masoretic Text in one word and differ in the next, and neither entry settles what the leather itself shows.

t: Leaders of men, or 'bites of men'?
p: The Greek has 'eight bites of men'. It seems to read the Hebrew word for 'princes' as a word for 'bite' or 'sting'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)

why: Nasikh 'prince' is a known word (Psalm 83:11; Joshua 13:21), and 'princes' fits 'shepherds' as leaders. The Greek dēgmata (bites) probably reflects the Hebrew root nashakh 'to bite', either from a different pointing of the same letters or a guess. It does not fit the context.
b: The Vulgate reads 'eight chief men' (octo primates hominum), following the Hebrew sense.

t: At its gates, in its trench, or with its spears?
p: The Hebrew 'bifthehah' means 'in its entrances'. The Greek has 'in its trench' and the Latin 'with its spears'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
Latin Vulgate (Jerome)

why: The Hebrew is clear and natural. The Greek word 'trench' is a translator's guess at a rare word, and the Latin appears to read the Hebrew in another way. The Murabba'at scroll has this word only in restored letters, so it cannot be cited.

a: like heavy showers on the grass
t: Showers on the grass, or lambs on the grass?
p: The Greek has 'like lambs on the grass'. The Hebrew has 'like heavy showers'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: like heavy showers on the grass

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and like lambs on the pasture grass

why: Showers belong with dew in the same line. The Greek 'lambs' does not match the Hebrew letters well and does not fit 'which put no hope in anyone'. It may be a translator's confusion over a rare word (revivim is found elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:2; Psalm 65:10; Jeremiah 3:3; 14:22).
b: The Qumran scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) preserves 'dew from the LORD' in these verses and differs from the Masoretic Text only in spelling (Ya'aqov with a waw, lo with a waw). The word for 'showers' is restored in both Qumran and Murabba'at texts.

t: Answer me, or testify against me?
p: The Greek and the Latin read 'answer me'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Vulgate

why: The Hebrew has the preposition be ('in, against'), which makes the legal reading 'testify against' natural in this courtroom. The Greek and Latin drop the preposition's force and read the plain 'answer'. Both fit; the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and gives the other in the note.
b: The Greek also adds a third question in verse 3: 'or how have I troubled you?'

t: Humbly, or 'ready'?
p: The Greek has 'be ready to walk'. The Hebrew has a rare word that is usually taken as 'humbly' or 'modestly'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Hebrew word is rare but has a known relative (tsanua', 'modest', Proverbs 11:2), and the Talmud and later Hebrew take it that way. The Greek 'ready' is a guess at the same word or a different text. 'Carefully' is a third rendering, the 'attentive' sense some modern lexicons give.
b: The Greek reads 'do judgment and love mercy and be ready to walk', and begins with 'if it has been told to you' as a question. No scroll preserves 6:8.

t: 'Wisdom sees your name', or 'he will save those who fear his name'?
p: The Greek and Latin turn this phrase into a promise to those who fear God's name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and sound wisdom sees your name

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ σώσει φοβουμένους τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and he will save those who fear his name
readings.plain: he will save those who fear his name

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.orig: et salus erit timentibus nomen tuum
readings.en: and salvation will be for those who fear your name
readings.plain: salvation will be for those who fear your name

why: The Masoretic Text is the hardest reading and cannot be shown to be a mistake. The Greek and Latin read one letter differently (yir'eh 'sees' becoming yir'e 'those who fear'), a simpler sense; this may be right, but the simpler reading is the kind a translator or copyist would supply. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and marks the line as difficult.

a: Is there still a wicked house
t: A wicked house, or fire in the house?
p: The Greek and the Latin read 'fire' in the house of the wicked. The Hebrew can be read 'is there still'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: is there still a wicked house
readings.plain: Is there still a wicked house

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Vulgate
readings.orig: μὴ πῦρ καὶ οἶκος ἀνόμου; adhuc ignis in domo impii
readings.en: is there not fire in the house of the wicked
readings.plain: Is there still fire in a wicked house

why: The Hebrew letters ha-esh can be ha-yesh 'is there?' (with a variant spelling) or esh 'fire'. The Masoretic Text reads 'is there', and it fits the question that follows. The Greek and Latin read 'fire' (a figure for judgment), a possible text. The Masoretes' reading is kept because the line is a question about the stored wealth.

a: Can I be clean with wicked scales
t: 'Can I be clean', or 'shall I count a cheat clean'?
p: The Hebrew has the LORD ask whether he himself can be clean. The Greek and Latin turn it into whether he will acquit a cheat.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: shall I be clean with wicked scales
readings.plain: Can I be clean with wicked scales

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: will the lawless be justified in the balance
readings.plain: Will someone with wicked scales be counted righteous

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.en: shall I justify a wicked balance
readings.plain: Shall I count as clean someone with wicked scales

why: The Masoretic Text reads a first-person verb in the qal ('I be clean'). The Greek and Latin, and many modern versions, change the pointing (ha'ezkeh to ha'azakkeh) to get 'shall I acquit'. The change is easy, and the sense ('I will not acquit a cheat') is clearer. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text because it makes sense as it stands: the LORD asks whether he can be called clean if he lets the cheating pass.
b: The Murabba'at scroll has these words only in restored letters.

t: A rare word: emptiness, darkness or humiliation?
p: The Hebrew word 'yeshachakha' appears nowhere else. The Greek says 'it will be dark', the Latin 'your humiliation'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (these letters are visible)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and it will be dark in you

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)

why: The word is a hapax legomenon (found once). A root that some link with 'be empty, hungry' fits the pairing with 'eat but not be full'. The Greek and Latin are guesses from context. The Murabba'at scroll reads the same consonants as the Masoretic Text.

a: The rules of Omri are kept
t: 'Are kept' or 'you kept'; Omri or Zimri?
p: The Hebrew verb is a rare passive form. The Greek has 'you kept the rules of Zambri' (Zimri).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (these words are visible)
readings.en: and the statutes of Omri are kept
readings.plain: The rules of Omri are kept

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and you kept the rules of Zambri
readings.plain: You have kept the rules of Zimri

why: The Masoretic Text is supported by Mur88 and is the harder reading (the verb form is unusual). Omri fits the sequel, 'the house of Ahab', his son. The Greek 'Zambri' is the Greek form of Zimri (1 Kings 16:9-20, a king who ruled seven days); in the Greek of Kings, Omri's name is spelled 'Ambri', so the Greek here may be a scribal slip or a different tradition.
b: The Greek of the whole line also reads 'you kept' (second person) instead of a passive.

t: My people, or the peoples?
p: The Greek says 'the disgrace of peoples'. The Hebrew says 'my people'. The Murabba'at scroll agrees with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (these letters are visible)
readings.en: and the disgrace of my people you will bear

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and you will take the reproaches of peoples

why: Mur88 reads 'my people', so the Masoretic Text is early. The Greek 'peoples' is a different pointing of the same letters (ammim for ammi). 'The disgrace of my people' can mean the shame the people bring on God's name, or the scorn God's people are met with; the Greek 'of the peoples' means scorn from the nations.

t: A bribe, or smooth words?
p: The Hebrew consonants can be read 'bribe' (shillum) or 'peace' (shalom). The Greek reads 'peaceful words'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Qumran scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) and Mur88 (the same consonants, with no vowels)
readings.en: and the judge, for the bribe

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)

why: Both Qumran scrolls have the same consonants as the Masoretic Text (no vowels, so they decide nothing about the vowels). The Masoretic pointing gives shillum 'bribe, payment', a known word for 'payment, recompense' (Hosea 9:7), related to shalmonim 'bribes' (Isaiah 1:23), and it fits the courtroom. The Greek takes the consonants as shalom (peace, in the sense of smooth talk). The Plain English Translation follows the pointing.
b: The Greek also reads the other lines differently ('it is the desire of his soul', and at the end 'I will take away their good things').

a: It will be a day to build your walls
t: A day to build walls, or days of smearing brick?
p: The Greek text of verses 11 reads quite differently, with 'brick' and 'wiping out'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the words for 'a day to build' are visible)
readings.en: a day to build your walls
readings.plain: It will be a day to build your walls

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: ἡμέρας ἀλοιφῆς πλίνθου, ἐξάλειψίς σου ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη
readings.en: days of the smearing of brick; that day is your wiping out
readings.plain: It will be days of smearing brick

why: The Greek is not a close rendering and I cannot rebuild its Hebrew with certainty. It does not fit a promise of restoration and is probably a translator's struggle with a hard text. The second half of the verse ('on that day the boundary will lie far away') the Greek reads as 'that day will wipe away your ordinances', again different.

t: Egypt, a fortress, or Tyre?
p: The Hebrew word 'matsor' can mean Egypt, a fortress, or sound like Tyre. The Greek has 'fortified cities' and 'Tyre'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the second matsor is visible)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: αἱ πόλεις σου αἱ ὀχυραί ... ἀπὸ Τύρου

why: Matsor for Egypt is attested (Isaiah 19:6; 37:25; 2 Kings 19:24), and the sequence Assyria, Egypt, River, sea, mountain (Assyria to Egypt to the Euphrates) is a recognizable list of Israel's neighbors. The Greek reads 'fortified' (the ordinary meaning of the same word) and 'Tyre' (tsor), and makes the cities objects of division; it also reads 'Assyrians' as the people dividing them.
b: The Greek of 7:12 is a quite different sentence: 'and your cities will yield to leveling and to division by Assyrians'.

t: Subdue or sink?
p: The Greek says 'he will sink our guilt'. The Latin has 'put away' (Clementine) or 'tread' (Nova Vulgata).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the verb is visible)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)
Latin Vulgate. The Clementine edition reads deponet; the Nova Vulgata is reported to read calcabit ('he will tread'). Only the Clementine reading is given here
readings.en: he will put away our guilt
readings.plain: He will put our guilt away

why: Mur88 reads the same verb as the Masoretic Text. Kavash 'subdue' makes a sequence with the sea: first pin the enemy, then throw him in the water. The Greek 'sink' fits the sea picture and may be a translator's smoothing. The Latin editions differ from each other and from the Hebrew verb.

t: 'Their' sins, or 'our' sins?
p: The Hebrew says 'all their sins'. The Greek and the Latin say 'all our sins'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus); Latin Vulgate
readings.orig: πάσας τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν; omnia peccata nostra

why: The Greek and Latin match the 'us' and 'our' of the lines before ('have compassion on us', 'our guilt'), which is the smoother sentence. The Hebrew 'their' is the rougher reading, and a translator or copyist is more likely to even out a sentence than to disturb it, so the Plain English Translation keeps 'their'. It may be deliberate: the speaker moves from the community ('us') to the sins of the whole people, or to the nations' sins in the sea. The Greek also makes the sins the subject of a passive verb ('will be thrown'), so the shift from 'he' to 'you' in this verse is a feature of the Hebrew only.

t: Ancient days, or 'the days before'?
p: The Greek has 'as in the days before'. Two scrolls from the Judean desert preserve this verse and agree with the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Qumran scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g); Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the last words of the verse are visible in both)
Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, mainly Codex Vaticanus)

why: Two scrolls from the Judean desert agree with the Masoretic Text on the last words of the book, and the Greek differs only by rendering the phrase freely. There is no reason to change it.
b: The Septuagint's 'truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham' is a normal Greek rendering of emet and hesed and reflects the same Hebrew.
